Increased effort intolerance and unable to walk to work supported by: 'I also used to walk to work, but recently I can't because... I feel like very short of breath' and 'No, I can't' when asked about exercise.
Patient states: 'recently I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave,' indicating working from home or sick leave due to symptoms.

History: 'Yes, I had asthma... I also had hay fever and asthma eczema as well.' 'It's quite bad.' 'Yeah, I take the asthma inhaler.' 'Yeah, sometimes' to hospital, and 'Few years ago. Like three or four years ago, I think' when asked when asthma stopped, indicating childhood asthma with inhalers and intermittent hospital visits and stopping regular meds 3–4 years ago.

Current pattern: 'Have you taken any medication? Doctor: I took sulbutomal.' 'Okay, so you, you normally take that, do you... Doctor: Normally, yeah.' 'How often... ? Doctor: Every few weeks.' 'What about when you exercise... ? Doctor: Yeah,' indicating salbutamol every few weeks and with exercise.

Patient reports cough but denies fever: 'I have cough... and I have a fever.' Later, when asked about temperature: 'Was it normal? Doctor: Yeah... What was your temperature? Doctor: 37.' The clinician interprets 37°C as normal, and there is no confirmation of a high fever; describing 37°C as a 'maximum recorded temperature' and implying fever is misleading.
'Have you coughed any phlegm up... ? Doctor: No,' indicating no sputum production.
'Any, any blood in there when you cough? Doctor: No, I don't think so,' supporting denial of hemoptysis.
'Any chest pain? Doctor: No chest pain? No,' directly supports no chest pain.
'Have you been woken up at night time at all? Doctor: No. Just daytime walking,' supporting no nocturnal respiratory symptoms.

'I also had hay fever,' confirms history of hay fever.

Medications: 'Do you normally take any asthma inhalers over the last few years? Doctor: Yes.' ... 'I took sulbutomal.' and 'Do you take any other medications? Doctor: No. Nothing else.' So current list is salbutamol only.
'Any allergies to medications? Doctor: No, no allergies,' supports no allergies.
Family history is not mentioned anywhere in the transcript, so stating it was not discussed is accurate.

'Do you drink any alcohol regularly? Doctor: Yeah, one glass.' 'How often... ? Doctor: One glass of wine every... Every two or three days,' matches one glass every 2–3 days.
'Who do you live with? ... Doctor: I live with my partner,' supports living with a partner.
'What's your job day to day? Doctor: I'm an engineer,' supports employment as an engineer.
'Did you say you checked your temperature already? ... What Was your temperature? Doctor: 37. Yeah,' supports self‑reported 37°C.

Clinician: 'it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma. It could be triggered by if there's more pollen around or there may be. You may have a viral infection causing it to get worse.' This acknowledges possible viral infection; saying 'with no signs of infection' contradicts the clinician's mention of viral infection as a cause.

Clinician recommends antihistamine but does not explicitly label 'allergic rhinitis'; transcript only notes 'I have hay fever as well' and 'take a regular antihistamine.' The diagnostic term 'allergic rhinitis' is not used.
Eczema is mentioned as past history: 'I also had hay fever and asthma eczema as well,' which the clinician acknowledges in history; noting it as historical is consistent.
Plan: 'if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like every four hours initially,' matches increasing salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours.
'Have you got a spacer at home? ... Doctor: No.' 'What I can do is I can prescribe you... a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently,' supports prescribing a spacer.

'I can prescribe you a peak flow meter so we can check your breathing level' and 'if you could record a value first thing when you wake up in the evening over the next week,' supports prescribing a peak flow meter and morning/evening monitoring for one week.

'The other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine, which you can get from the pharmacy. I can put a suggestion on your notes,' matches recommending a regular antihistamine from the pharmacy.

'it would be a good idea, when you're feeling better, if we could arrange just a review... You can arrange a review in a week or so. But before that, if you're feeling worse.' This supports planning a follow‑up around one week.
'if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straight away,' supports advising to seek care if fever or wheeze worsens.
